messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadine is a 21-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who came to treatment several months after a military trauma that she still describes in concrete, sensory fragments rather than as a story she can easily tell straight through. She had enlisted young and had been proud of being able to handle technical work under pressure. During her service, one nighttime incident stayed with her in a way that made the dark itself feel altered afterward. She recalls being outside after dark in a high-alert setting when the atmosphere shifted abruptly from routine vigilance to immediate danger. What remains most vivid to her is the combination of darkness, the strain in her body as she tried to move quickly and stay prepared, and the sense that the night concealed threat in every direction. Since then, she has felt that once the sun goes down, safety becomes uncertain and too much can happen before she has time to react.

In the period after the trauma, Nadine returned to civilian life and resumed work as a database administrator, a role that suited her in some ways because of its order and predictability. She spends much of the day managing systems, checking for errors, and making sure data are where they are supposed to be. Even so, the structure of the job has not quieted her sense that things can become dangerous very quickly. She has become especially careful about anything that feels like physical strain. If a task leaves her winded, raises her heart rate, or creates the kind of bodily tension she associates with being on alert, she pulls back from it. She avoids workouts that used to seem ordinary, takes stairs only if she feels she has no alternative, and is quick to stop any activity that makes her body feel taxed. To her, this is not simple preference. She has come to see bodily stress as a warning sign, too close to the state she was in that night, and she does not trust what might happen if she lets herself get there again.

Her apartment has gradually become the place where this need for control is most visible. Nadine cleans and organizes repeatedly, often far beyond what is necessary. She wipes down counters that are already clean, straightens objects until they line up exactly, and reorders drawers and shelves after she has already finished. When she describes this, she does not frame it as excessive so much as necessary. If everything is in place, if surfaces are clean and nothing is out of order, she can breathe a little easier. Disorder unsettles her. A cup left out, shoes by the door, papers not stacked properly can create a sharp internal agitation, as though small signs of disarray mean she is no longer fully on top of things. After work she may spend long stretches cleaning instead of resting, and if she tries to stop before it feels complete, she becomes tense and distracted, circling back to the task until the room looks exactly right.

Night has become the clearest line in her life. Nadine avoids going out after dark whenever she can. She schedules errands for the morning or early afternoon, declines invitations that would keep her out in the evening, and watches the clock in winter when daylight fades early. At work, this means she tries to leave before sunset and becomes uneasy if a database problem threatens to keep her in the office late. On one recent evening, a systems issue required the team to stay past normal hours. As the windows darkened, she found it increasingly hard to concentrate on the troubleshooting in front of her. She kept thinking about getting to her car in the dark, about open parking lots and the vulnerability of being outside at night. She left as soon as she could, embarrassed by how urgent it felt, then spent part of the night cleaning her apartment kitchen and reorganizing a hallway cabinet until she felt settled enough to sleep.

Over the weeks and months, these habits have narrowed her life. She is single and has grown more isolated without fully intending to. Friends have stopped asking her out for evening meals as often because she usually says no or leaves early. Colleagues know her as competent and meticulous, but some have noticed she is unwilling to stay late or join after-work gatherings. Nadine is aware that her world has become smaller and more controlled, yet she also feels certain there is a reason for each rule she has made. What frightens her most is not simply remembering the military incident, but the idea of being caught off guard again—outside at night, physically strained, without any way to impose order.

She sought help after realizing how much effort it was taking to organize her life around these limits. A recent stretch of late-day work demands and repeated comments from others that she seemed constantly on edge forced her to see that she was structuring nearly every day around avoiding darkness, avoiding bodily strain, and restoring order whenever she felt unsettled. She arrived to treatment wanting relief, though cautiously. She says she hopes to feel “normal” enough to go through a day without planning around sunset or cleaning to calm herself, but she is afraid that if she lets go of any of these precautions, she will be exposed again to the same kind of danger she faced before.
